  the parser executes it while the rest of the document is still being parsed —
  early enough that the row never paints at scrollLeft 0 first. The equivalent
  positioning in useButtonNavScroll runs on mount, which is after that first
  paint, so on its own it produces a visible jump (see TECH-1574).

  The row is centred on whichever item was active on the *previous* page, so it
  carries on looking exactly as the reader left it. When they have moved to a new
  section, useButtonNavScroll then animates from here to the new active item —
  which is why this must not centre that item itself. On the first page of a
  session there is nothing recorded, so the active item is centred directly.

  Centring is idempotent, so a page carrying two navs (and therefore two copies
  of this script) simply re-measures an already-positioned row for no effect.

  Deliberately measured rather than delegated to `scrollIntoView`, which also
  scrolls the element's vertical ancestors and would move the page itself.

    document.querySelectorAll('[' + listAttribute + ']').forEach((list) => {
      const scrollKey = list.getAttribute(listAttribute);
      const lastActiveItem =

      // The recorded item may no longer be in this nav — the header's overflow
      // links, for one, all collapse into a single "More" trigger with no href.
      const lastLink =
        lastActiveItem && list.querySelector('[href="' + lastActiveItem + '"]');
      const target =

        list.querySelector('[' + activeItemAttribute + ']');

      if (!target) return;

      const listRect = list.getBoundingClientRect();
      const targetRect = target.getBoundingClientRect();
      const distanceFromCentre =

        (listRect.left + listRect.width / 2);

Read our Privacy notice Andy Burnham could slash up to £200 off energy bills when Britons can expect a surge in gas and fuel prices this winter due to the Iran war. Ofgem’s energy price cap will rise by four per cent in October, due to an increase in wholesale gas prices as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up the cost of supplying energy in the UK. This means the annual figure will rise from £1,663 to £1,723 – equivalent to around £5 more per month, or £60 per year, but analysts are already predicting a bigger hike to the price cap in the new year. The prime minister, who has repeatedly claimed that he hopes to ease the cost of living, is reportedly exploring options to subsidise the millions of households living in fuel poverty, including those who do not currently qualify for existing support. open image in gallery Andy Burnham has promised to ease the cost of living for Britons ( PA ) A support scheme called the Energy Price Protection Payment (EPPP) could be implemented in January, The Telegraph has reported, which would aim to mitigate the impact of the rising prices. The paper reported that the EPPP would apply to recipients of the warm homes discount, as well as others deemed in need of support. Claimants would have to receive benefits, according to the paper, but it remained unclear whether it would cover the estimated additional 2.5 million households classed as being in fuel poverty. No final decision has reportedly been made on how much the EPPP support would be worth, or whether to proceed with it. A government spokesperson did not deny the reports but emphasised the VAT cut on electricity bills already being implemented, which is expected to take around £45 off the Ofgem price cap from October, as well as the £150 removed from bills in April. Go to website ADVERTISEMENT open image in gallery Energy bills are expected to rise in October ( PA ) They said: “The chancellor is fully focused on giving families and businesses breathing space and helping ease cost pressures. “That’s why we have removed VAT from electricity bills and are reducing electricity costs by up to 25 per cent for more than 10,000 manufacturing businesses through our British industrial competitiveness scheme.” The government has also expanded the £150 warm home discount to around six million households, extending the scheme for the rest of the decade. Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK. We welcome the government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter. “Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap, and many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for electricity consumed out of peak times. “It's also worth considering different payment methods, with prepayment customers paying the lowest price cap rates, and could save consumers an average of about £45 compared to direct debit.” More about Energy Bills Energy price cap Conflict Andy Burnham gas prices Join our commenting forum Join thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their replies Comments Most popular Popular videos Bulletin Read next Get in touch Contact us Our Products Subscribe Register Newsletters Today’s Edition Install our app Archive Other publications International editions Independent en Español Independent Arabia Independent Turkish Independent Persian Independent Urdu The Standard Extras Puzzles All topics Free bets offers Latest deals Competitions and offers Independent Advertising Independent Ignite Syndication Working at The Independent Legal Code of conduct and complaints Contributors Cookie policy Privacy policy User policies Modern Slavery Statement Thank you for registering Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in

  Runs as a blocking inline script placed immediately after a nav's markup, so
  the parser executes it while the rest of the document is still being parsed —
  early enough that the row never paints at scrollLeft 0 first. The equivalent
  positioning in useButtonNavScroll runs on mount, which is after that first
  paint, so on its own it produces a visible jump (see TECH-1574).

  The row is centred on whichever item was active on the *previous* page, so it
  carries on looking exactly as the reader left it. When they have moved to a new
  section, useButtonNavScroll then animates from here to the new active item —
  which is why this must not centre that item itself. On the first page of a
  session there is nothing recorded, so the active item is centred directly.

  Centring is idempotent, so a page carrying two navs (and therefore two copies
  of this script) simply re-measures an already-positioned row for no effect.

  Deliberately measured rather than delegated to `scrollIntoView`, which also
  scrolls the element's vertical ancestors and would move the page itself.

  `listAttribute`, `activeItemAttribute` and `storagePrefix` are injected by the
  wrapping IIFE.

try {
  if (window && document) {
    document.querySelectorAll('[' + listAttribute + ']').forEach((list) => {
      const scrollKey = list.getAttribute(listAttribute);
      const lastActiveItem =
        scrollKey && sessionStorage.getItem(storagePrefix + scrollKey);

      // The recorded item may no longer be in this nav — the header's overflow
      // links, for one, all collapse into a single "More" trigger with no href.
      const lastLink =
        lastActiveItem && list.querySelector('[href="' + lastActiveItem + '"]');
      const target =
        (lastLink && lastLink.closest('li')) ||
        list.querySelector('[' + activeItemAttribute + ']');

      if (!target) return;

      const listRect = list.getBoundingClientRect();
      const targetRect = target.getBoundingClientRect();
      const distanceFromCentre =
        targetRect.left +
        targetRect.width / 2 -
        (listRect.left + listRect.width / 2);

      // `behavior: 'instant'` is required — the list sets
      // `scroll-behavior: smooth` in CSS, which scrollTo honours otherwise.

Read our Privacy notice Sri Lanka’s Supreme Court has overturned a presidential pardon granted to a hardline Buddhist monk and asked him to return to prison. Galagodaatte Gnanasara, a top member of the Bodu Bala Sena (BBS) or "Buddhist Power Force", was sentenced to six years in prison by the court of appeal after being found guilty of contempt of court. He was also found guilty of intimidating Sandya Eknaligoda, the wife of political cartoonist Prageeth Eknaligoda, who was forcibly disappeared in 2010. Gnanasara interrupted a court hearing in 2016 over the abduction of the cartoonist in which military intelligence officials were accused. He shouted at the judge and lawyers because the military officials had not been allowed bail, and threatened Eknaligoda’s wife. Eknaligoda was critical of the former president Mahinda Rajapaksa , a nationalist who justified the brutal end to the civil war in 2019 by portraying himself as the nation’s spiritual saviour. Gnanasara served less than a year of his prison sentence before the then president Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him. The apex court on Thursday ruled that the presidential pardon was "arbitrary" and declared it invalid, while ordering the monk to return to serve the rest of his prison sentence. The pardon was challenged by Ms Eknaligoda along with Colombo-based non-profit organisation Centre for Policy Alternatives. The BBS, led by Gnanasara, has been accused of stirring up violence against Muslims and Christians, mainly in Buddhist-dominated parts of Sri Lanka. The monk has denied these allegations. The monk has faced accusations in cases regarding anti-Muslim violence, hate speech, and defaming the Quran. Sirisena’s successor, Gotabaya Rajapaksa, appointed Gnanasara to a presidential task force to draft proposals on legal reforms, a move that faced widespread criticism. In 2024, he was sentenced to four years in prison for inciting hatred against Muslims during a 2016 press conference. He was later granted bail. A year later, he was sent to nine months in prison for insulting Islam and inciting religious hatred.
